body:
In article <x4hyam2m1ww.fsf@Steam.Stanford.EDU>,
  John McCarthy <jmc@Steam.Stanford.EDU> wrote:
> I have been brooding over TK's claim that scientists are pretending
> when they claim to be motivated by curiosity and are motivated instead
> by career considerations.  I'll claim that curiosity is a substantial
> motivation for me and hence, by courtesy, for other scientists.
>
> As for the work I write papers about, it would be hard to verify a
> claim that it was motivated by curiosity.  However, I read articles
> and puzzle over problems about which I can never hope to write a
> paper.  So do many other people, both scientistsf and others.

Par 87 - 92 The motives of scientists
http://www.cs.umass.edu/~ehaugsja/unabom/docs/manifesto.toc.html

I agree that TK is projecting.  But...

Isn't TK's point that one would not brood over scientific topics if one had
interesting things to do directly related to food, shelter, clothing?  TK
wouldn't probably argue that you're curious.  He just doesn't find your
curiousity to be "legitimate".	But somehow his intellectual interest in
language IS legit.  I guess he doesn't exclude himself from his arguments. 
He probably figures he'd lose interest in many of the things he does if he
"had a wife and children".

Great line in Annie Hall (I think that's the one) about this general
idea which I think I've mentioned before.

There are only scientists, artists, and other specialized lines of work in
the world because we no longer have the satisfaction (stress?) of hand to
mouth existence.  Well... 10 or 20% of the world doesn't...

"If the chemist and the entomologist had to exert themselves seriously to
obtain the physical necessities, and if that effort exercised their
abilities in an interesting way but in some nonscientific pursuit, then
they wouldn't give a damn about isopropyltrimethylmethane or the
classification of beetles."

- Par 87
